title: A surge in outages has experts questioning whether it’s a glitch or cyberattack | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

Shortly before 4 p.m. on a busy Friday afternoon, with airports crowded with weekend travelers, the Federal Aviation Administration announced a nationwide ground stop on all flights. Federal officials would later explain an antiquated system was being overhauled and the radio communications network that guided thousands of flights had become “unstable,” prompting the shutdown.

The ground stop order came just asMicrosoft was sayingit was restoring service to its “365” customers after a massive outage caused by a technical issue – and not long beforeWorkday, a payroll provider, also experienced a service outage related to a technical issue.

Earlier that afternoon,the FBI had issued an urgent noticeto private-sector cybersecurity chiefs that was the sum of many fears about AI and its darker applications.

Under a bright yellow banner reading “FBI FLASH,” the agency warned of ARTEX, a product initially designed for companies to be able to attack their own systems to search for vulnerabilities that cyber criminals or hostile foreign powers could exploit. The FBI notice warned that the very people ARTEX was designed to protect against had obtained it and turned it into a weapon.

“Since at least August 2026, a variety of malicious cyber actors have used ARTEX to conduct campaigns targeting organizations globally across multiple sectors, including financial services, government, technology, defense, semiconductor, energy, healthcare, manufacturing, telecommunications, and legal industries,” the FBI warning reads.

As a senior official in the Analysis Division at the Director of National Intelligence a few years back, I used to read through the firehose of intel in the daily reports. It was more than one could digest, but I would look for patterns, events that came in clusters, similar things that begged the question: Could this all be coincidence?

The last few days have reminded me of that natural suspicion.

By Monday afternoon,United Airlines suffered a technical shutdownthat grounded flights andChase and Wells Fargo banksboth had issues with consumers being able to access accounts online.

So far, none of the cyber incidents that occurred in just 100 hours since last week have been classified as the work of foreign adversaries or cyber criminals, but to eliminate any possibility takes time. Even cybersecurity experts who accept the explanations of companies and government officials that these incidents all occur from technical glitches are struck by the sudden surge of these cascading failures, some on a massive scale, and back to back.

The hijacking of the ARTEX hacking tool is not the first time an application designed to detect security weaknesses has been used by malicious actors, but ARTEX, falling into the wrong hands, has advanced the threat exponentially.

“ARTEX significantly reduces the time required to chain attack techniques, with some intrusions progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours,” the FBI warning states. “The framework enables threat actors with minimal technical expertise to conduct complex, multi-target operations simultaneously, fundamentally accelerating attack velocity and expanding operational scale.”

ARTEX can be directed to do the kind of work that takes advanced hackers days or weeks: conduct reconnaissance on a website, spray for passwords, find vulnerabilities that had not been addressed with security patches, or locate open ports. With a system like ARTEX doing the work, nations and criminal groups could have the ability to conduct sophisticated cyberattacks even without a significant investment in the technical skills historically required for such operations.

“That is democratization of cyberattacks and cybersecurity,” said Elizabeth Buckley, the head of Cyber and Technical Solutions at Teneo consulting.

“Used in the proper context, when we use AI tooling as one of the good guys, we can very quickly find our own exploits, our own weaknesses and patch them. So, I don’t mean to create a doomsday scenario,” Buckley said. “ARTEX is particularly interesting that it has been leveraged by bad actors significantly in the last few weeks.”

Recently, ARTEX was used in an attack against South Korean financial institutions and a supply chain compromise that affected ConnectWise Cloud Backup customers, according to the FBI’s warning.

“This is now moved beyond the capabilities or capacity of a human being,” said Prashanth Mekala, former assistant special agent in charge of the FBI’s Counterintelligence & Cyber Division in New York and chief security officer for ROKT, the global e-commerce and tech company.

Mekala said the AI-powered tools being hijacked by malicious actors are moving faster than most company’s security teams can react.

“The defenders have to be able to adapt to the speed at which the threat actors move, which is daunting. But if you were able to leverage the capacity of these AI tools, which is a tremendous amount of capacity, that gives your team a fighting chance,” he said.

But that means companies must spend more on cybersecurity – an idea many are resistant to, especially if they haven’t suffered an attack that resulted in a serious loss.

On Monday, FBI agents took possession of the router believed to be behind the Friday meltdown so agents can examine it to determine if there’s anything unusual about how it functions. The following day,an FAA spokesperson told CNNthe agency is pausing the installation of new Juniper telecommunications routers – which are part of the FAA’s ongoing upgrades – as it investigates the ground stop.

In July 2024, the cybersecurity company Mandiant reported that Chinese threat actors had achieved backdoor access to Juniper routers, prompting the company to launch its own investigation.

“The team determined that the set of six implants are indeed malicious software designed to remotely take over Junos OS devices,” Juniper wrote in an advisory, adding customers should check their routers or upgrade to the newer models.

While there is no evidence that the router involved in the FAA incident was compromised, the fact that Juniper – which is working on a major US government critical infrastructure upgrade – has been targeted by Chinese actors before is more than enough to have the FBI looking at it very carefully.

Ask any intelligence official how to destabilize a culture, country or confidence in government and they will tell you:target transportation, communications, and financial systems. And detection is more complicated than it once was. US cybersecurity experts point to state actors using a technique known as “living off the land,” or LOTL, where foreign government cyber teams disguise their tools so they can live within critical systems and appear as normal processes.

In February 2024, a trio of federal agencies warned organizations involved in infrastructure such as water, power, and communications that Russia and China were already hiding within critical US infrastructure.

“The authoring agencies have observed cyber threat actors, including the People’s Republic of China (PRC) and Russian Federation state-sponsored actors, leveraging LOTL techniques to compromise and maintain persistent access to critical infrastructure Organizations,” the FBI, National Security Agency and Department of Homeland Security wrote in the document.

“LOTL enables threat actors to conduct their operations discreetly as they can camouflage activity with typical system and network behavior, potentially circumventing basic endpoint security capabilities,” the agencies said.

That shows it may take a deeper dive for the FAA, banks, internet service providers, and cellular companies to be able to say with certainty that all these recent disruptions were normal system failures – particularly when the weapons designed to make systems fail may look just like the real parts that make the systems work.

Gus Rodriguez, the former commanding officer of the NYPD Cyber Intelligence team assigned to the FBI’s New York Task Force, believes cybersecurity has to be seen as a local threat, not just one for the federal government.

In 2014, Rodriguez organized the chief information security officers for hospitals, water, power, phones–anything that New York City could not afford to have fail during a crisis, or where their failurewould bethe crisis. They met regularly and went over detailed cyberthreat intelligence to protect their systems. They were briefed not just on the latest threats to their systems but also given information so they could hunt for adversaries in the shadows of their own networks. New York City then created its own cyber command to cover more than 100 city agencies – a model Rodriguez believes other states, counties and cities should emulate.

“As AI gets faster, as cyberattacks get faster, what are we doing to make sure that critical infrastructure operators in America are sharing that information as fast?” Rodriguez said. “Because as we already know, 85% of critical infrastructure in America is owned and operated by the private sector.”

Experts were divided about their level of certainty regarding whether there was anything nefarious behind these recent failures, though each was struck by the sudden spike in major incidents. But they all agreed that corporate America is going to have to bite the bullet and spend more in an area that will not add to their profits but could keep them from losing everything.

Any serious organization will need the equivalent of a cyber-MRI, Teneo’s Buckley said.

“You say, okay, well, are the right people in place for general due diligence, right? Do you have a Chief Information Security Officer? Do you have the right security people? Are the right compliance measures in place? So just get those basic boxes checked first,” she said. “And then the second thing that you look at is, say – technology aside – what is the thing that materially breaks this company? What is the existential crisis that could occur that breaks this company? Because the fact is, all material risk sits in data somewhere.”

CNN’s Nicki Brown and Eric Levenson contributed to this report.
